ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: When is machine learning a better fit than hand-written rules?
options: When the logic is fully specified by regulation and must be exact
When the pattern is too complex to write down as rules, but many labelled examples exist
When you have very little data and need guaranteed behaviour
When the output must be identical for every input
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: ML pays off when rules are hard to state (spam, image recognition, ranking) but examples are plentiful. Exact, regulated logic is better as code: it is cheaper, auditable and deterministic.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: What does 'training' a model actually do?
options: It writes if/else rules that a developer then reviews
It copies the training data into the model so it can look answers up
It compiles the model into faster machine code
It adjusts the model's parameters to reduce its error on example data
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Training is optimisation: tune weights so predictions match the examples (lower loss), aiming to generalise to new inputs. Merely memorising the data is overfitting, not the goal.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: You need to compute sales tax for orders across jurisdictions with published rates and rules. Which approach fits best?
options: Deterministic code driven by a rules/rates table
A neural network trained on past invoices
A clustering model that groups orders by region
A reinforcement learning agent rewarded for matching tax filings
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: The rules are known, must be exact and must be auditable, so code is right. An ML model would only approximate them and could be wrong on unusual cases with no explanation.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: Which phrase best captures the difference between traditional programming and machine learning?
options: Traditional programs run on CPUs; ML programs run only on GPUs
Traditional programming handles numbers; ML handles text
Traditional programming: rules + data produce outputs. ML: data + expected outputs produce the rules (a model)
Traditional programs are deterministic; ML models can never be deterministic
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: In ML the program's behaviour is learned from examples rather than written by hand. Hardware and data type aren't the distinction, and a trained model with fixed weights can be fully deterministic at inference.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: A spam classifier trained two years ago has slowly lost accuracy, even though the code hasn't changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model's weights decay slowly over time
Data/concept drift: spam tactics and email patterns changed, so live data no longer looks like the training data
The server's CPU is slower now
The model forgot rarely used patterns because of garbage collection
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Models assume production data resembles training data. Spammers adapt and language changes, so performance drops. Monitor live metrics and retrain on recent data. Stored weights don't change on their own.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: What is the difference between a model's parameters and its hyperparameters?
options: Parameters are set by hand; hyperparameters are learned from data
They are two names for the same thing
Parameters are the inputs at inference time; hyperparameters are the outputs
Parameters (e.g. weights) are learned during training; hyperparameters (e.g. learning rate, tree depth) are chosen before training
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Training fits the parameters; you choose hyperparameters, often by comparing validation scores. Inputs at inference are features, not parameters.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: A fraud model returns 0.83 for a transaction. As the backend engineer integrating it, how should you treat that number?
options: As a score to compare against a threshold chosen from the business cost of false positives vs false negatives
As proof that the transaction is fraud
As the percentage of the amount that is fraudulent
As meaningless unless it is exactly 0 or 1
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Model outputs are scores (sometimes calibrated probabilities). The decision threshold is a product choice: block, review or allow, based on what errors cost. A score of 0.83 isn't certainty.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: Which problems are good candidates for machine learning? Select all that apply.
options: Predicting which customers are likely to churn from their usage history
Detecting near-duplicate product listings with slightly different text
Validating that an email address has the right format
Computing an invoice total from line items
Recommending articles a user is likely to read
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Churn, fuzzy duplicates and recommendations are pattern problems with no clean rules. Email format checks and invoice totals are exact logic that plain code does better.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: Which statements about putting an ML model into production are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Training data should represent the data the model will see in production
A model can learn biases present in historical labels
More data always fixes a model trained on wrong labels
Model performance should be monitored after deployment because it can drift
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: Representative data, attention to label bias and monitoring are basic requirements. More data with systematically wrong labels just teaches the wrong thing more confidently.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: A machine-learning model is guaranteed to be correct on inputs that are similar to its training data.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: False. Models are statistical and make errors even on familiar-looking inputs; they're judged on error rates measured on held-out data, not guarantees.

ai-ml-basics:0.prompt: A large language model is a machine-learned model: its behaviour comes from parameters fitted to data rather than from hand-written rules.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:0.explanation: True. LLMs are neural networks whose billions of weights are learned by training on text (then fine-tuned). Prompts steer them, but the underlying behaviour is learned.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: You want to predict a house's sale price from features like size, location and age, using past sales with known prices. What kind of problem is this?
options: Unsupervised clustering
Supervised regression
Reinforcement learning
Supervised classification
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: There are labelled examples (known prices) and the target is a continuous number, so it's supervised regression. Classification would predict a category, such as 'will sell within 30 days'.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: Marketing wants to group customers into segments by behaviour, with no predefined segment labels. Which approach fits?
options: Unsupervised learning, e.g. clustering such as k-means
Supervised classification
Reinforcement learning
Linear regression
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: There are no labels, and the goal is to find structure in the data, which is unsupervised clustering. Classification needs labelled examples of each segment.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: A program learns to play a game by trying moves and receiving points for winning and penalties for losing. Which learning paradigm is this?
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Self-supervised learning
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: An agent acting in an environment and learning from rewards is reinforcement learning. Nobody labels the correct move for each position, which supervised learning would need.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: You have past card transactions labelled 'fraud' or 'legitimate' and want to flag new ones. What type of task is this?
options: Supervised regression
Unsupervised dimensionality reduction
Reinforcement learning
Supervised binary classification
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: Labelled examples with two categories make it binary classification. The model may output a score, but the target is a class, not a continuous quantity as in regression.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: You want to detect unusual behaviour in server metrics, but you have almost no labelled incidents. Which approach is most practical?
options: Supervised classification trained on the handful of labelled incidents
Unsupervised or semi-supervised anomaly detection that models normal behaviour and flags deviations
Reinforcement learning rewarded for detecting outages
Linear regression predicting the number of incidents per day
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: With few positive labels, learn what 'normal' looks like and flag outliers. A classifier trained on a few incidents will overfit them and miss new failure types.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: LLM pre-training predicts the next token of huge amounts of text, with no human labelling. What is this usually called?
options: Self-supervised learning: the labels come from the data itself
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised clustering
Fully supervised learning with human labels
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: The 'label' (the next token) is taken from the text itself, so no annotators are needed. It's trained like supervised learning but without human labels, hence 'self-supervised'.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: What is RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) as used to tune chat models?
options: Humans write every answer the model will ever give
The model is retrained from scratch on human conversations only
A reward model is trained on human preference rankings of responses, and the LLM is optimised to maximise that reward
Users' thumbs-up clicks directly update the weights in real time
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: Humans rank candidate outputs, a reward model learns those preferences, and an RL algorithm (e.g. PPO) nudges the LLM towards higher reward. It's an offline training stage, not live updates from clicks.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: Which of these are unsupervised learning tasks? Select all that apply.
options: k-means clustering of customers
PCA to reduce 100 features to 10
A logistic regression spam classifier trained on labelled emails
Discovering topics in a pile of unlabelled documents
Linear regression predicting prices from past sales
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: Clustering, dimensionality reduction and topic modelling find structure without labels. The spam classifier and the price regression both learn from labelled targets, so they're supervised.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: Which statements describe reinforcement learning? Select all that apply.
options: The agent learns from a reward signal that may arrive long after the actions that caused it
It involves a trade-off between exploring new actions and exploiting known good ones
It requires a labelled correct action for every state
The agent's own actions influence the data it sees next
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: Delayed reward, exploration vs exploitation, and actions shaping future data are what define RL. Needing the correct action for every state would make it supervised learning.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: Supervised learning needs training examples that include the correct output (label).
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: True. The model learns the mapping from inputs to the labelled outputs. Without labels you're in unsupervised or self-supervised territory.

ai-ml-basics:1.prompt: Clustering algorithms like k-means tell you what each cluster means, such as 'high-value customers'.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:1.explanation: False. k-means only assigns points to groups (and you even choose k). People interpret the clusters by inspecting their members and statistics.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: You're building a model to predict whether a subscriber will cancel within the next 30 days. What is the label?
options: The subscriber's number of logins last month
The subscriber's plan type
Whether the subscriber actually cancelled within 30 days of the snapshot date
The model's predicted probability of cancelling
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: The label is the true outcome you want to predict. Logins and plan type are features (inputs), and the predicted probability is the model's output, not ground truth.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: What is the difference between training and inference?
options: Training fits the model's parameters on examples; inference uses the trained model to predict on new inputs
Training happens on the user's device; inference happens in the data centre
Training uses features; inference uses labels
They are the same step run with different batch sizes
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: Training is the expensive, usually offline optimisation step. Inference is running the fixed model per request or in batches. Inference doesn't use labels; you don't have them for new data.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: A churn model scores 0.99 AUC offline but performs poorly in production. One feature is account_closed_date. What is the most likely problem?
options: The model is underfitting
The test set was too large
The learning rate was too low
Target leakage: the feature encodes the outcome and isn't available at prediction time
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: A closure date only exists after the customer churns, so offline it gives the answer away and in production it's empty. Only use features available at the moment the prediction is made.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: Features were normalised in a Python training pipeline, but the Node.js service that calls the model computes them with slightly different logic. Accuracy in production is much lower than offline. What is this called, and what's the fix?
options: Overfitting; add regularisation
Training-serving skew; share a single feature-computation path (or a feature store) between training and serving
Class imbalance; oversample the minority class
Concept drift; retrain weekly
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: The model sees differently computed inputs at serving time than in training. Reusing the same transformation code or artefacts fixes it. Retraining on schedule doesn't help if serving still computes features differently.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: Why is encoding a 'country' feature as integers (US=1, IN=2, DE=3, ...) a problem for a linear model?
options: Integers use more memory than strings
Linear models can't accept integer inputs
It implies an order and distance between countries that doesn't exist; one-hot encoding (or embeddings) avoids this
It makes the model train too quickly
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: A linear model would treat DE as 'three times' US, a meaningless relationship. One-hot gives each category its own weight. Tree models are less sensitive to this, but it's still a poor default.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: Why are features often standardised (e.g. to mean 0, standard deviation 1) before training models like k-NN or gradient-descent-based regressions?
options: So features on large scales don't dominate distances or gradients, and optimisation converges faster
So the model can handle missing values
Because labels must be between 0 and 1
To make the dataset smaller on disk
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: Income in dollars would swamp age in years in a distance calculation and skew gradient steps. Scaling puts features on comparable footing. It doesn't handle missing values, and it's unrelated to the label range.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: A Node.js API loads a 500 MB model file from disk inside each request handler before running a prediction. Latency is terrible. What is the right fix?
options: Retrain a smaller model with fewer features
Move the model file to a faster SSD
Increase the request timeout
Load the model once at startup (or lazily once) and reuse it for all requests
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: Inference should only run the forward pass; loading weights is a one-time cost. Keep the model in memory (or in a dedicated model server). A faster disk still pays the load cost on every request.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: You're predicting food delivery time at the moment an order is placed. Which are valid features? Select all that apply.
options: Distance between restaurant and customer
The restaurant's historical average preparation time
Time of day and day of week
The actual delivered-at timestamp
The rating the customer gives the courier after delivery
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: Valid features must be known at prediction time. The delivered-at timestamp and the post-delivery rating only exist afterwards, so they leak the outcome.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: Which statements about inference are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Model weights are normally frozen during inference
Inputs must go through the same preprocessing as during training
Inference needs the labels of the new data
Batching requests on a GPU can raise throughput at the cost of some latency
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: Inference runs a fixed model on consistently preprocessed inputs, and batching trades latency for throughput. Labels for new data are unknown; that's why you're predicting.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: A label is the value a supervised model is trained to predict.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: True. Features are the inputs; the label (target) is the known answer for each training example that the model learns to reproduce.

ai-ml-basics:2.prompt: Adding more features always improves a model's accuracy on new data.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:2.explanation: False. Irrelevant, noisy or leaky features can cause overfitting or production failures, and they add cost. Feature selection is judged on validation performance.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: What is a loss function in model training?
options: A function that removes bad training examples
A number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are, which training tries to minimise
The percentage of data lost during preprocessing
The time it takes to train one epoch
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: The loss scores the gap between predictions and labels (e.g. squared error, cross-entropy). Gradient-based training repeatedly changes parameters to make it smaller.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: In one step of gradient descent, how are the parameters updated?
options: Set to random values and kept if the loss improves
Moved in the same direction as the gradient
Moved opposite to the gradient of the loss, by a step scaled by the learning rate
Set to the average of all previous parameter values
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: The gradient points towards steepest increase, so w = w - learning_rate * gradient moves downhill. Moving with the gradient would increase the loss.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: During training, the loss jumps around wildly and eventually becomes much larger than at the start. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too high, so steps overshoot the minimum
The learning rate is too low
The model has too few parameters
The validation set is too small
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: Oversized steps bounce across the valley and can diverge. A learning rate that is too low gives slow, steady progress, not explosion.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: Training loss goes down extremely slowly and is still falling steadily after many epochs. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Lower the learning rate further
Remove the loss function
Shuffle the labels
Increase the learning rate moderately (or use a schedule/adaptive optimiser)
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: A smooth but slow decrease suggests steps that are too small. A larger learning rate or an adaptive optimiser like Adam speeds convergence; lowering it further makes things slower.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: Which loss function is standard for binary classification when the model outputs a probability?
options: Mean squared error
Binary cross-entropy (log loss)
Mean absolute error
Hinge loss on the raw probability
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: Cross-entropy heavily penalises confident wrong predictions and pairs naturally with a sigmoid output, giving good gradients. MSE/MAE are regression losses; hinge loss is used with SVM margins, not probabilities.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: A regression dataset has a few extreme outliers in the target. How do mean squared error and mean absolute error compare?
options: They behave identically
MAE is more affected because it uses absolute values
MSE is more affected, because squaring makes large errors dominate; MAE is more robust
Neither can be used when outliers exist
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: An error of 10 contributes 100 to MSE but 10 to MAE, so MSE bends the fit towards outliers. Huber loss is a common compromise.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: Why is mini-batch stochastic gradient descent used instead of computing the gradient on the full dataset every step?
options: Each step is much cheaper and fits in memory, and the gradient noise can help escape poor regions, at the cost of noisier updates
It always reaches a better minimum than full-batch gradient descent
It doesn't need a learning rate
It removes the need for a loss function
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: Mini-batches give a cheap, unbiased estimate of the gradient, so you get many more updates per unit of compute. They don't guarantee a better minimum, and they still need a learning rate.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: You minimise f(w) = (w - 3)^2 with gradient descent, starting at w = 0 with learning rate 0.1. What is w after one step?
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: f'(w) = 2(w - 3) = -6 at w = 0. The update is w = 0 - 0.1 * (-6) = 0.6, a move towards the minimum at 3. -0.6 comes from adding the gradient instead of subtracting it.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: Which statements about gradient descent are correct? Select all that apply.
options: On non-convex losses (like neural networks) it can settle in a local minimum or saddle region
Standard gradient descent needs a loss that is differentiable (almost everywhere)
It always finds the global minimum
An epoch is one full pass over the training data
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: Gradient descent follows local slope, so only convex problems guarantee the global minimum. It needs gradients, and an epoch means seeing every training example once.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: Training loss becomes NaN after a few steps. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.
options: A learning rate so high that weights explode
Taking log(0) in a hand-written cross-entropy without an epsilon or clipping
Unscaled input features with huge values
Training for too few epochs
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: Exploding updates, log of zero and huge inputs all produce inf/NaN numerically. Too few epochs leaves the loss high but finite.

ai-ml-basics:3.prompt: The gradient of the loss points in the direction of steepest increase, which is why gradient descent subtracts it.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:3.explanation: True. To reduce the loss you step in the negative gradient direction; the learning rate sets how far.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: A model has high error on both the training set and the validation set, and the two errors are similar. What does this indicate?
options: Overfitting
Underfitting: the model is too simple or under-trained to capture the pattern
Data leakage from validation into training
A perfectly tuned model
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: If it can't even fit the training data, it lacks capacity or training (high bias). Overfitting shows low training error and much higher validation error.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: What is the held-out test set for?
options: Tuning hyperparameters until the score is as high as possible
Training the final model with more data
A final, unbiased estimate of performance, used once after model selection is done
Replacing the validation set to save data
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: The validation set (or cross-validation) is for choosing models and hyperparameters; the test set is reserved for the final check. Tuning on it makes its score optimistic.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: A team tries 200 hyperparameter configurations and picks the one with the best score on the test set, then reports that score. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; that's what the test set is for
200 configurations is too few to be meaningful
They should have used training accuracy instead
The reported score is optimistically biased because the test set was used for selection; use a validation set or cross-validation and keep the test set untouched
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: Picking the best of many on one dataset overfits to that dataset's noise. The test set is then no longer independent, so the number overstates real-world performance.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: A decision tree reaches 100% training accuracy but does poorly on validation. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Limit tree depth or prune it (or use an ensemble like a random forest)
Remove the depth limit so it can grow further
Evaluate on the training set instead
Add an ID column as a feature
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: An unrestricted tree memorises the training data. Constraining depth, setting a minimum leaf size or averaging many trees reduces variance. An ID column gives it more noise to memorise.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: You're forecasting next week's demand from daily sales history. A colleague randomly shuffles all days into train and test. Why is this a problem?
options: Random splits are too slow for time-series data
The model sees days from the future of the test period during training, leaking information; split chronologically instead
Shuffling changes the labels
Test sets for time series must be larger than training sets
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: In production you only ever have the past. A chronological (or rolling-origin) split mimics that; random splits let the model use neighbouring future days and inflate scores.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: Your dataset has many rows per user (one per session), and you randomly split rows into train and test. Test accuracy looks great but production accuracy on new users is poor. What is the likely issue?
options: The test set is too small
The model is underfitting
The same users appear in both train and test, so the model recognises users rather than generalising; split by user (group split)
The learning rate is too high
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: Rows from one user are highly correlated, so random row splits leak identity-specific patterns into the test set. A GroupKFold or user-level split measures performance on unseen users.

options: Splits the data into k folds, trains k times with each fold held out once for validation, and averages the scores
Trains k different model types on the full dataset
Repeats training k times on the same split to reduce randomness
Uses k% of the data as the test set
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: Every example gets used for validation once, which gives a more stable estimate, especially with limited data. It costs k training runs.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: Which techniques typically reduce overfitting? Select all that apply.
options: L2 regularisation (weight decay)
Dropout in neural networks
Early stopping when validation loss stops improving
Greatly increasing model capacity with no other change
Continuing to train after validation loss starts rising
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: Regularisation, dropout and early stopping all limit how closely the model fits noise. More capacity and training past the validation minimum make overfitting worse.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: A model suffers from high variance. Which statements typically apply? Select all that apply.
options: There's a large gap between training and validation performance
Its predictions change a lot when trained on a different sample of data
More training data usually helps
Its training error is high
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: High variance means overfitting: it fits training data well, is unstable across samples, and benefits from more data or regularisation. High training error is the mark of high bias.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: The test set should be used to choose a model's hyperparameters.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: False. Hyperparameters are chosen on validation data or with cross-validation; the test set is held back for a final, unbiased estimate.

ai-ml-basics:4.prompt: If training and validation error are both high and close together, adding more training data alone is unlikely to help much.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:4.explanation: True. That's high bias: the model can't represent the pattern. A richer model, better features or less regularisation help more; extra data mainly helps high variance.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: What does precision measure for a classifier?
options: Of all actual positives, the fraction the model found: TP / (TP + FN)
The fraction of all predictions that were correct
Of all predicted positives, the fraction that are actually positive: TP / (TP + FP)
How consistent the model's predictions are across runs
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: Precision asks: when the model says 'positive', how often is it right? TP / (TP + FN) is recall, and the fraction of all predictions that were correct is accuracy.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: In a dataset where 99% of transactions are legitimate, a model labels every transaction 'legitimate'. What are its accuracy and its recall for fraud?
options: Accuracy 99%, fraud recall 0%
Accuracy 1%, fraud recall 100%
Accuracy 99%, fraud recall 99%
Accuracy 50%, fraud recall 50%
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: It's right on every legitimate case (99% accuracy) but catches no fraud (TP = 0, so recall = 0). This is why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: A classifier produces TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 40 on a test set. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.5, recall 0.8
Precision 0.8, recall 0.8
Precision 0.5, recall 0.5
Precision 0.8, recall 0.5
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: Precision = 40 / (40 + 10) = 0.8. Recall = 40 / (40 + 40) = 0.5. F1 = 2 * 0.8 * 0.5 / 1.3 ≈ 0.62. Swapping FP and FN in the formulas gives the reversed (0.5, 0.8) answer.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: For an email spam filter, users are furious when real emails land in the spam folder, but they tolerate some spam in the inbox. Which metric should you prioritise for the 'spam' class?
options: Recall
Precision
Accuracy
Training loss
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: Real email marked as spam is a false positive, and precision penalises false positives. Pushing recall would catch more spam but move more real mail into spam.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: You raise a classifier's decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.9. What typically happens?
options: Precision and recall both increase
Recall increases and precision decreases
Precision tends to increase and recall decreases
Neither changes, because the model is the same
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: A stricter threshold predicts positive less often, so fewer false positives (precision up) but more missed positives (recall down). The threshold moves you along the precision-recall trade-off.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: A model has precision 1.0 and recall 0.1. Why is its F1 score about 0.18 rather than 0.55?
options: F1 is the harmonic mean, which is pulled towards the smaller value, punishing imbalance between precision and recall
F1 also includes accuracy, which is low here
F1 is the product of precision and recall
F1 is capped at 0.2 when recall is below 0.2
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: F1 = 2PR / (P + R) = 2 * 1.0 * 0.1 / 1.1 ≈ 0.18. The arithmetic mean (0.55) would hide that the model misses 90% of positives. The product would give 0.1, not 0.18.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: With a highly imbalanced dataset (0.1% positives), why is the precision-recall curve often more informative than the ROC curve?
options: ROC curves can't be computed for imbalanced data
PR curves are always higher than ROC curves
ROC curves ignore the decision threshold
ROC's false-positive rate is divided by a huge number of negatives, so many false positives barely move it, while precision exposes them
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: FPR = FP / (FP + TN). With millions of TNs, ROC AUC can look excellent while most flagged items are false alarms. Precision shows that directly. Both curves sweep the threshold.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: Which metrics use true negatives (TN) in their formula? Select all that apply.
options: Accuracy
Specificity (true negative rate)
False positive rate
Precision
Recall
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all; specificity = TN / (TN + FP); FPR = FP / (FP + TN). Precision and recall use only TP, FP and FN, which is why they suit rare-positive problems.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: A model is used as the first-stage screen for a serious disease, with positives sent for a more accurate follow-up test. Which statements are sensible? Select all that apply.
options: High recall is the priority, so few true cases are missed
False positives are more acceptable because the follow-up test catches them
Optimising accuracy alone is enough
Lowering the decision threshold increases recall
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: A missed case is costly and false alarms get filtered later, so favour recall, typically by lowering the threshold. With a rare disease, accuracy would reward a model that predicts 'healthy' for everyone.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: Recall is calculated as TP / (TP + FN).
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: True. Recall is the share of actual positives the model caught. TP / (TP + FP) would be precision.

ai-ml-basics:5.prompt: On the same dataset, a model with higher accuracy always has a higher F1 score.
options: True
False
ai-ml-basics:5.explanation: False. Accuracy counts true negatives and F1 ignores them. On imbalanced data, a model that predicts mostly negatives can have higher accuracy but much lower F1.
